title: What if you were shrunk to 1 cm tall?
caption:
Big raindrops would weigh more than you. 🌧️🤏

Shrink a 70 kg person to 1 cm tall (175× smaller) and they'd weigh about 13 mg. A big 5 mm raindrop is about 65 mg.

Falls stop mattering: air resistance caps your speed at about 4 m/s, instead of about 53 m/s at full size.

But you'd lose body heat about 175× faster per kilo, because your skin area shrinks more slowly than your mass.

And getting wet becomes the real trap: the film of water clinging to you would weigh about as much as you do.

Send this to the friend who's always cold.

A new impossible experiment every day.

⚠️ Don't try this. Falls that are harmless for an insect can seriously injure or kill a full-size person.

#science #physics #whatif #sciencefacts #biology #rain #scaling #theimpossiblelab
sources: https://cabinetmagazine.org/issues/28/haldane.php (J.B.S. Haldane, 'On Being the Right Size', 1926: air resistance is proportional to surface, a mouse survives a 1,000-yard mine-shaft drop; a man leaving a bath carries a ~1/50-inch water film weighing ~1 lb; a wet mouse carries about its own weight of water; small animals need food proportional to surface)
https://gpm.nasa.gov/category/faq-category/precipitation (NASA GPM: raindrops up to ~6 mm diameter, ~8 mm reported; largest fall at ~10 m/s)
https://hypertextbook.com/facts/2001/IgorVolynets.shtml (raindrops 0.1–5 mm typical; drops unstable above ~5.5 mm)
https://hypertextbook.com/facts/1998/JianHuang.shtml (skydiver terminal speed, arms and legs out: ~53 m/s / 192 km/h; 54–56 m/s in other references)
Computed: scale factor 1.75 m / 1 cm = 175; mass 70 kg / 175^3 = 13.1 mg; 5 mm drop = (4/3)π(2.5 mm)^3 × 1 mg/mm^3 = 65.4 mg (4 mm = 33.5 mg, 3 mm = 14.1 mg)
Computed: terminal speed ∝ √(mass/area) ∝ √L at constant drag coefficient: 53 m/s × √(1/175) = 4.0 m/s (≈14 km/h, running pace); direct drag estimate (Cd 1, frontal area 0.7 m² scaled) gives ≈3 m/s
Computed: surface/volume ratio ∝ 1/L, so heat loss per kg rises ×175 at equal skin temperature and heat-transfer coefficient (geometric scaling, first-order)
Computed (Haldane's film): 0.45 kg film / 70 kg body = 0.65 %; film ∝ L², body ∝ L³ → ×175 → ≈1.1× body mass at 1 cm
